title: "Linux host"
description: "Building the library, udev rule, and the Raspberry Pi bench host"

Linux is the [recommended lab host](index.qmd#host-operating-system): the
jitter observed on the reference bench is typically 1–2 µs, against more
frequent schedule restarts and device overruns on macOS. Setup takes two
steps — a one-time udev rule, and building `arduino-io` from source — and
both are the same whether the host is a desktop, a laptop or a Raspberry Pi.

## Install the udev rule

Without it, USB device nodes for the board are only writable by root, so
`arduino-io` and the driver need `sudo` for every call. The rule grants
access to the logged-in user instead. From a clone of ArduinoDriver repository:

```bash
sudo cp extras/driver/etc/99-arduino-usbio.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
```

Then unplug and replug the board. The rule file itself says:

```
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="2341", MODE="0666", TAG+="uaccess"
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="2e8a", MODE="0666", TAG+="uaccess"
SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="303a", MODE="0666", TAG+="uaccess"
```

It grants access to every USB device carrying one of the three vendor IDs
ArduinoDriver probes: Arduino (`2341`), Raspberry Pi Foundation (`2e8a` —
this covers RP2040-based boards, not a Raspberry Pi single-board computer
used as host) and Espressif (`303a`). `TAG+="uaccess"` gives the logged-in
seat user an ACL through `systemd-logind`; `MODE="0666"` also covers systems
without `logind`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Skipping the rule

Without the rule installed, every `arduino-io` invocation (and any program
linking `arduino_driver`) needs `sudo` to open the board. That is fine for a
one-off check but not for a lab bench a student runs unattended.

:::

## Build and install `arduino-io`

You need `git`, CMake 3.24 or newer, and a C++ compiler (`g++` or `clang`,
e.g. `sudo apt install build-essential`):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver.git
cd ArduinoDriver
cmake -B build -DARDUINODRIVER_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build --config Release
cmake --install build --config Release --prefix ~/.local
```

The first build fetches its dependencies (libusb, `fmt`, `cxxopts`) via
CMake's `FetchContent`, so it takes a few minutes. `arduino-io` ends up in
`~/.local/bin` — make sure that directory is on your `PATH`, or install to
`/usr/local/bin` instead (needs `sudo`):

```bash
sudo cmake --install build --config Release
```

Confirm it works:

```bash
arduino-io list
```

## Using a Raspberry Pi as the bench host {#raspberry-pi}

A Raspberry Pi is just a Linux machine with USB ports, so everything above
applies unchanged: install the udev rule, install `build-essential` and
`cmake` from the distribution's package manager, build `arduino-io` the same
way. Because it is small, quiet and cheap enough to dedicate one per bench, a
Raspberry Pi (or a similar single-board computer) is a practical way to give
every bench a Linux host without a full desktop machine.

::: {.callout-note}
## Not independently verified on ARM

ArduinoDriver's own continuous integration builds and tests the driver on
Linux, macOS and Windows runners (all x86_64); it does not currently include
an ARM/Raspberry Pi job. The CMake build is portable C++20 with no
architecture-specific code in the parts a bench uses, so it is expected to
build the same way — but treat a Raspberry Pi build as something to verify on
your own bench with the [verification procedure](verify.qmd), not as
independently confirmed by upstream CI.

The specific Raspberry Pi model to standardize on for AMLab benches is
Raspberry Pi 5 (4Gb).

:::

## Why Linux for AMLab

At maximum rate in bulk mode the board samples from `loop()`, not a hardware
timer, so the *host's* own USB scheduling is part of what determines the
timestamps a stream actually records. Linux's USB stack gives the most
consistent scheduling of the three host operating systems characterized so far,
which is why it is the recommended host for any acquisition where timing matters
— see [Setting up a bench](index.qmd#host-operating-system) for the numbers.

Reducing the sampling rate below the board's maximum (e.g. 20 kHz on a Portenta
H7) uses the internal MBED OS clock and is typically very precise (within µs) if
not completely accurate and drift free.
